blocks.text: Dear Ms. Johnson:

This letter sets down the terms on which our firm will act for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} in the redesign of the way it delivers its services, and it becomes our agreement at the moment you countersign the enclosed copy and return it to me. I have written it at some length and in plain language, in the belief that an engagement of this kind proceeds more steadily when both sides have read the same words and can point to them afterward, and I would ask you to weigh each paragraph against the conversation from which it comes and to tell me, before you sign, wherever it fails to match what you understood us to have agreed.
The Work We Have Agreed to Undertake

The assignment is a redesign of the way {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} delivers its services to the customers it serves, and its object is an arrangement that carries the work through more reliably and at a cost the organization can defend, without unsettling the parts of the present operation that already serve those customers well. We will begin by establishing a faithful account of how service is delivered today, following the work as it actually moves rather than as the written procedures describe it, and only once that account is agreed will we form a view about how the work might be delivered differently.

Our manner of working is deliberate and, I hope, plain in the way it presents itself. We proceed from your own evidence rather than from a template, on the understanding that the value of the work lies in getting your particular question right and not in supplying a general answer that would fit any company equally and yours no better than the rest; and where the ground shifts under the analysis, as it commonly does once the work is genuinely under way, we will return to you and adjust the plan with you and not around you.
The Team That Will Carry the Work

Jason Torres, a Principal of the firm, will own the relationship with you and will be the person to whom you bring any question of consequence; he is accustomed to telling a client what the evidence shows rather than what is most comfortable to hear, and you should expect that of him. Working alongside him, Julie Vasquez will carry much of the underlying research and the comparison sets against which we test what we find, and she keeps every source labeled so that any figure we place before you can be traced back to where it came from. I will keep my own hand on the engagement at the points where a judgment must be made about how far a conclusion can be pressed before it outruns what we actually know, and nothing of consequence will leave the firm under our name without my having read it first.
Fees and Payment

Our fee for the engagement as I have described it is {{fact:f:E-2020-001.fee}}, which covers the time of the people named above through the expected completion of the work. We will render invoices against that amount as the engagement proceeds, each payable within thirty days of your receipt of it. The fee covers our people and their time and not the incidental costs of the work, such as travel or the reproduction of materials, which we will incur only with your agreement and pass through to you at what they cost us; and should the shape of the work change materially from what this letter contemplates, I will raise the question of the fee with you and we will settle it together before any further work begins, so that nothing reaches you on an invoice as a surprise.
Term and Termination

The engagement begins on {{fact:f:E-2020-001.start}} and is expected to run for something on the order of seven months, though we will treat it as complete when the work is genuinely done and not merely when the calendar has turned. Either of us may bring it to an end on fourteen days' written notice to the other; and should you choose to do so, you will owe us for the work properly performed to that point and for any costs already committed on your behalf, and for nothing beyond that.
Confidentiality

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} in the course of this work we will hold in confidence and use solely for the purposes of the engagement. That obligation binds every member of our team, it survives the end of the work, and it extends to the fact of our involvement as fully as to its substance. We ask the same of you in respect of the methods and written materials we bring to the assignment, which represent the firm's own way of working.
Limitation of Liability

We will perform the work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect of a firm engaged for it, and we stand behind what we do. We do not, however, govern the decisions your leadership will ultimately take on what we recommend, nor the conditions of the markets in which your business operates, and so, save to the extent the law does not permit such a limit, our liability to you arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees paid under it.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our firm is established, and any dispute arising under it will be determined by the courts of that state. Should any single provision of this letter be held unenforceable, the remainder of it will continue in force, unaffected.

If this letter reflects the understanding we reached, I would be grateful if you would sign one copy where indicated below and return it to me, keeping the other for your own file. Once your signed copy is in hand, Jason Torres will write to fix the first meetings and the initial requests for information; until then, you are welcome to reach me, Julie Ramsey, directly with anything the letter leaves open.

The aim of this engagement is a service delivery model for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} that carries the work through more reliably and at a cost the organization can defend, and this memo sets out how the team will divide the work to get there. The engagement commenced on {{fact:f:E-2020-001.start}} and is expected to run about seven months; our sponsor on the client side is Melissa Johnson, the General Manager, and Jason Torres will hold the single point of contact with her so that the client hears one voice from us. In these first weeks we are after one thing only, which is a faithful picture of how service is delivered today, traced from the work as it actually moves; recommendations come later, and only once the client has agreed the facts they rest on.
How the work divides

items: Current-state map. I will document how service moves through the organization today, function by function, from the intake of a request to its completion, drawing on the existing process documentation and a short round of interviews with the people who actually run the work.

Delivery baseline. I will assemble a clean baseline of volumes, cycle times, and the cost of delivery from the client's own records, so that any recommendation we make later rests on figures both sides accept rather than on impressions.
Comparison set. I will build the outside reference points against which we will test what we find, keeping each source labeled so that a comparison can be checked rather than taken on faith.

Client interviews. Jason Torres will set the schedule of conversations with Melissa Johnson and the managers who own the delivery process, so that the current-state picture reflects how the work is done and not only how it is described.

Working file. We will keep one shared engagement file from the first week, so that every figure and source can be traced, and so that our notes to the client draw from a single record rather than from anyone's memory of it.

blocks.text: Immediate steps

For the coming week the priority is access and materials. I will send the client team the first request for information by the end of this week, and I will begin the comparison set in parallel so that we are not idle while the data comes in. Before we meet again, I need one thing from each of you, which is the list of documents and contacts your part of the work will require, sent to me by Friday, so that I can fold it into a single request to {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} rather than several arriving out of step. Once that is in hand I will circulate the consolidated request and a short index of what we have received and what is still outstanding, and Jason Torres will confirm the cadence of the standing check-ins with Melissa Johnson.
Hi Melissa,

The service delivery review for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} is moving on schedule, and I wanted to give you a short update and line up the next batch of materials. Jason Torres and I went through the first cut of the intake and cycle-time data this week; the early read is the familiar one, that the process runs tidier on paper than the people doing the work describe it to be, which is exactly what the next round of data should let us pin down.

To move from that first read to a baseline we can stand behind, two things from your side would help: read access to the last two years of the delivery-cost records that sit behind the operating budget, and thirty minutes each with the two managers your team flagged as the ones who really run the process. If either needs a sign-off on your side, point me to the right person and I will approach them directly rather than put it back on your desk.

For the file, I have logged you, Melissa Johnson, as our contact of record on this thread, so that anything you send back reaches the whole team at once. You can reach me, Julie Vasquez, directly for anything touching the data, and Jason Torres for anything touching scope or pace; between us we will keep the review on its timeline.
Sincerely
Minutes of the Working Session: Service Delivery Redesign for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}

These minutes record the working session held with the client team to review the current-state findings for the service delivery redesign and to agree what the next phase of the work should pursue for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}.
Attendees

items: 1. Jason Torres, Principal, Calderwood Partners (chair)
2. Julie Vasquez, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
3. Melissa Johnson, General Manager, {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}

blocks.text: Matters discussed

The session opened with a review of the current-state work, which is now largely complete. Julie Vasquez took the group through the map of how service moves through the organization today and through the baseline of volumes, cycle times, and delivery cost she has assembled from the client's own records, and she was careful throughout to distinguish the figures the two sides have reconciled from the handful still being checked against source. The group agreed that the map confirms what the early interviews had suggested, namely that the delays cluster at the handoffs between functions rather than within any single one of them, and that this is the pattern the redesign will have to address before any other.

Julie Vasquez also presented the first of the outside reference points she has been assembling, noting where the organization's cycle times sit against them and, more usefully, where the comparison does not hold because the underlying work differs; the group agreed that these references would be used to test the eventual redesign rather than to set a target in the abstract, and asked that each be kept with its source so that a number can be run back to its origin later. There followed a discussion, left deliberately open at the close, of how far the apparent slack in the process could actually be recovered.

Melissa Johnson cautioned that some of that apparent slack reflects commitments to particular customers that cannot be unwound quickly, and the group accepted that the redesign should separate the changes available in the near term from those that depend on such commitments running their course. It was agreed, as a matter of method, that nothing would be presented to the client's leadership as a recommendation until the baseline is fully reconciled and both sides have signed off on the figures on which it rests.
Actions agreed

rows: Close out the figures still being checked against source and finalize the delivery baseline
Frame the redesign questions as choices for the client's leadership, keeping the analysis and the recommendation clearly separate
Confirm which customer commitments constrain the near-term changes and name who on the client side can speak to them

blocks.text: The next working session will be scheduled once the baseline is reconciled. These minutes will stand as the record of what was agreed unless a correction is raised within the week.
Status Report: Service Delivery Redesign for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}
Prepared by Julie Vasquez for the leadership of {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}, covering progress since the last report.
Where things stand

The engagement is on schedule and on budget, and the work has reached the point where the current-state picture is settled and the design of the new service model has begun. The team holds a reconciled baseline of how {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} delivers service today, the leadership has agreed the facts that baseline rests on, and the questions the redesign turns on are now framed clearly enough to work against. Nothing on the horizon threatens the timeline, though two items set out below will need attention to keep it that way.
Progress this period

items: The current-state map is complete and has been reviewed with the client team, and it locates the main delays at the handoffs between functions rather than inside any one of them.
The delivery baseline of volumes, cycle times, and cost is reconciled, with both sides agreed on the figures behind it.
The comparison set is assembled, with each outside reference kept against its source so that it can be checked rather than taken on faith.
The redesign questions have been framed and agreed with the client team as the focus of the next phase.

blocks.text: The budget

The engagement is being carried out against a fixed budget of {{fact:f:E-2020-001.fee}}, and roughly half of that has been consumed to date, which tracks the point the work has reached. The remaining budget is sufficient for the design and validation still ahead, and Jason Torres will flag it at once should the scope shift in a way that would change that judgment; as matters stand, no change to the fee is contemplated, and none is expected.
The work ahead

Over the coming weeks the team moves from describing the current model to designing its replacement. In practice that means setting out two or three options for how service could be delivered, testing each against the reconciled baseline and the comparison set, and bringing them to the leadership as choices to weigh rather than as a single answer handed down. Jason Torres will hold the standing check-ins through this phase, and I will keep the shared engagement file current so that any figure behind an option can be traced back to where it came from.
Risks and watch items

items: A small number of customer commitments constrain how quickly parts of the process can change. The design will separate the moves available in the near term from those that depend on those commitments running their course, so the client can begin where it is able.

Two of the delivery managers whose input the design depends on have limited availability over the coming weeks. Scheduling their sessions early is the surest way to keep the design phase from slipping.

blocks.text: The single thing that would most help from the client's side in the next two weeks is confirmed time with those two delivery managers; with that on the calendar, the design phase can proceed on its current timeline.
Working Session Minutes: Service Delivery Redesign for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}

These minutes record the working session held to review the near-final recommendations for the service delivery redesign and to settle what remains before the engagement closes for {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}.
Present

items: 1. Jason Torres, Principal, Calderwood Partners (chair)
2. Julie Vasquez, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
3. Melissa Johnson, General Manager, {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}

blocks.text: Summary of discussion

The session opened with a walk-through of the recommended model, which has now taken close to its final form. Julie Vasquez presented the validation of the design against the reconciled baseline, showing where the redesigned handoffs are expected to remove delay and, with the same care she has kept throughout, marking the two estimates that still rest on assumptions the client will want to test in operation rather than on paper. The group agreed that the recommendation is sound enough to put before the client's leadership, provided those two assumptions are stated plainly rather than folded quietly into the headline figures.

Before turning to implementation, the group reviewed the engagement against its timeline and agreed that the work remains on course to close on schedule, with the analytical effort substantially behind it and the remaining work concentrated in drafting and review. Jason Torres observed that this is the point at which a team is most tempted to keep polishing an analysis that is already firm enough to act on, and asked that the effort now go into making the recommendation usable to the client rather than into refining figures that will not change the decision.

Discussion then moved to implementation, on the understanding that a redesign the organization cannot absorb is of little use however well it reads. Melissa Johnson set out which of the changes her teams could take up in the near term and which would have to wait on the customer commitments identified earlier in the work, and the group agreed that the final deliverable should present the redesign in two phases accordingly, so that the client can begin where it is able without waiting on the parts that are constrained. It was further agreed that the engagement would close with a written recommendation and a short implementation plan, the changes themselves remaining the client's to carry into effect.
Actions and owners

items: 1. Finalize the recommended model and mark the two open assumptions clearly for the client to test in operation. Owner: Julie Vasquez.
2. Structure the final deliverable in two phases, separating the near-term changes from those constrained by existing customer commitments. Owner: Jason Torres.
3. Confirm on the client side which teams will own each near-term change and identify the commitments that fix the timing of the rest. Owner: Melissa Johnson.

blocks.text: The next and likely final working session will be set once the draft recommendation has been circulated. These minutes will stand as the record of what was agreed unless a correction is raised within the week.
